utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we return to the evidence of Mr. Akhavan, can I explain what I'd intended to be the witness position today, something I'd intended to tell you on Friday but there wasn't time to do so. There's a witness called Williams, whose summary you have, who I believe is unable to stay overnight because of business commitments in England, and my plan had been for him to arrive on the early plane this morning to be started, basically, whenever he arrived, and for him to return the same day, because I was confident that by dealing with his evidence in chief, swiftly and efficiently, that would be possible. I had intended, with your leave, to call Mr. Akhavan to continue with his evidence until such time as Williams arrived. Unfortunately, Williams missed the plane this morning in Manchester, altogether, and the next plane that he can be on would not bring him here much before, I think, 12.30. I'm making inquiries to see whether he is in fact prepared to stay overnight, given the problems that have been caused, and, if so, then there would be a day of evidence available for him, starting at about 12.30 or 1.00, until tomorrow, providing, of course, that the Court were prepared to interpose him notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Akhavan's evidence would be part heard. There are always problems with witnesses coming from overseas, and this particular witnesses is quite important -- that is, Williams is quite important -- is probably always going to express the same attitude towards overnight stays on any other occasion, so it's a problem we have. May I, in principle, communicate to him that if he comes and is prepared to stay overnight, we'll try and conclude his evidence between today and tomorrow at lunchtime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Akhavan has already taken the solemn declaration. We were at paragraph 15 of his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I have one short matter I would like to take up once the witness is through. It's concerning the question related to fighting in built-up areas that was posed to me last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, at a convenient moment, we can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us the last time you were giving evidence, Mr. Akhavan, about a contribution to a meeting by the man Ante Valenta, and I think after that, did you meet Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards I was taken by members of the British Battalion to meet Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts, what was he doing, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly where the building was situated except that it was somewhere in Vitez, and we -- I met with Mario Cerkez, initially, with myself and a member of the British Battalion who was accompanying me throughout my trip, and I began to ask him about the events which transpired on the 16th of April in the region of Vitez, focusing, obviously, not on Ahmici and other areas which may not have been under his control, but on Vitez, where apparently, according to his own statements, where he was the commander of the HVO forces. He informed me that he was asleep on the morning of April 16th when the hostilities began in the region of Vitez, but that he was not entirely surprised, because they had anticipated possible hostilities with Bosnian Muslim forces in the area. Halfway through the meeting, Colonel Bob Stewart joined us, and we began to discuss more specifically the duties of commanders in general in dealing with such situations. And both Bob Stewart and I informed Mr. Cerkez that it would be his responsibility to conduct a thorough investigation into the matter, and, if necessary, to discipline and ensure the prosecution of his subordinates for violations of humanitarian law in the Vitez region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did he say of what his troops were doing, as he understood it, what, if anything, did he say about any alleged involvement of his troops?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez simply suggested that when the attack began on the morning of the 16th, that chaos reigned in the Vitez area, and that he was not necessarily in control of everything that was happening, that he was at home at the time. He did not, to the best of my recollection, deny that any atrocities had taken place, but we did not have a detailed discussion about that, except that I informed him that according to the padre of the British Battalion, the overwhelming majority of casualties in Vitez were Bosnian Muslims, and that there were only a handful of Bosnian Croat casualties, and that many of the Bosnian Muslims who were killed were women, children, elderly people, who most probably were not killed in a combat-related sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did he say about what his troops were doing, or what he thought they were doing, and whether they were involved?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My impression was that he suggested that his troops were simply defending themselves against --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- against Bosnian Muslim forces in an attack which they may not have fully anticipated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he acknowledge any involvement by the men of the unlawful acts that you were suggesting had occurred?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not to the best of my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his general manner or demeanour when he was speaking to you or to Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say that initially, during the first half of the interview, that there was a somewhat confrontational attitude between myself and Mr. Cerkez. When Colonel Stewart appeared and we began to speak about his individual responsibility for conducting investigations and suggesting that he may actually be held liable, I think that my impression was that he appeared somewhat more intimidated than he had in the first part of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Intimidated in what sense, how manifested?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: His general disposition, his demeanour, from what I could observe, was that of someone who was concerned about possibly being held liable or accountable for the acts of killing and other violations against civilians in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it was on the same day that I had met Mr. Cerkez and Blaskic. I don't recall exactly what day that was, possibly May 3rd or 4th, towards the end of my stay in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We met him, I believe, in Busovaca. It was outside of Vitez at his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been trying to meet him before the day when you actually met him or was this a meeting at first attempt?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I recall, we had asked the members of the British Battalion to arrange a meeting for us and we had left it really in their hands. It may have been that they had tried calling him perhaps one or two days prior to the meeting, but eventually we met in what appeared to be a contemporaneously arranged meeting, because we were held waiting outside his office for more than an hour, from what I recall, prior to getting an audience with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was instrumental from BritBat in getting that audience?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a member of the British Battalion whose name escapes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes back to you, if it does -- or I can put it to you if it's not challenged. I don't know. Was it Major Dundas-Whatley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a young man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was known by you of Kordic's role at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told by most of the people that I spoke with that he was the most senior and influential figure in the Bosnian Croat leadership in the Lasva Valley region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What offices did you know him to hold or believe him to hold?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was told, and this was confirmed during my meeting with him, that he was vice-president of the HDZ political party and of the HVO as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, how was he dressed? By whom was he accompanied?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was wearing military fatigue, as I recall, and he was in a room or in a building which was heavily fortified. There were, I would say, several armed men in the building with him, apparently HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in the room where you met him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that in the room itself also, there were a couple of armed HVO soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you confront him with the allegation about Ahmici and the HVO's responsibility for it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was the essence of my meeting with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His reaction, first of all, in general terms, if you will, in emotional terms?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In general terms, he categorically denied any involvement on the part of the HVO, suggesting that this crime could not have been committed by his soldiers. He instead suggested that Bosnian Serb soldiers may have penetrated the region under the cover of night and committed these atrocities, or alternatively that the Muslims themselves may have committed the atrocities in order to provoke international sympathy. The general demeanour of Mr. Kordic, I would say that the best word I can think about is somewhat arrogant, and I did not recognise any serious concern with the account of atrocities which I shared with him. I think the attitude simply was that, "We have not done it," and when the explanations that he offered were not satisfactory, I suggested to him that he would need to try harder to persuade me that the Bosnian Croats themselves, the HVO forces, were not responsible. He suggested that he would try his best to come up with an even better explanation. I did not sense at that point in time that there was any concern or any desire to offer a serious explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he offer you any particular reason why his men could not have done this thing?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: One of the reasons which I recall was simply a suggestion that his men, as good Christians with high ethical standards, would never be able to commit such acts. That was really the only explanation that I was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the question of investigating the attack raised with him?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I, as I had done with Mr. Cerkez and Blaskic, reminded Mr. Kordic that as an individual with senior responsibility in that region, that he should inquire into these allegations, that he could conduct a comprehensive investigation and ensure that those who may have committed these crimes are brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His reaction, if any, to that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Kordic was not pleased by the fact that I was trying to tell him what to do. I think the idea was that he was the man in charge and that he would do as he pleased. But I think that the idea of an investigation to him did not seem necessary, because as he had said to me categorically that the HVO could not have been involved, therefore, there was really no need to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this discussion with you, did he identify anybody superior to him to whom you should turn, for example, Blaskic, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Clearly not. I think it was very clear from my conversation with him and from my conversations with Blaskic and Cerkez that he was the man in command in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently visit Ahmici in company with Ambassador Thebault and other high ranking officials, including Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall, the day following my meeting with Mr. Kordic, we returned to the village of Ahmici together with Ambassador Thebault as well as three ambassadors representing the European Community, from the U.K., France, and Spain respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the video Z1626.1 please be played? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we see from that video, were you present with the delegation when four charred bodies, including two apparent children, were discovered?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. That was the visit, as I explained, with the three EC ambassadors and Ambassador Thebault. The bodies which we discovered were based on the testimony of one man, I believe, by the name of Sakib Ahmic, who my colleague, (redacted), had interviewed the previous day, and he had given us exact directions to his home. He had apparently been hiding behind a sofa --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to any double hearsay from this gentleman, Sakib Ahmic, who was apparently interviewed by Mr. Akhavan's colleague, Your Honour, and not by Mr. Akhavan. So Mr. Akhavan did not actually hear any descriptions that may or may not have been given by Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do we really need this part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it's particularly necessary, although I'm not sure that it's objectionable either, but I'm quite happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else arising from the film that you want to cover or comment on that we haven't yet touched upon? In the nature of the discoveries that you made, you found the four bodies. Anything else that you found that we haven't yet touched upon?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I think I, in my testimony earlier, had indicated the extensive destruction which we had witnessed in the village of Ahmici, and in this particular case, I don't think there's anything to add really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On completion of your tour, did you, with (redacted), draft a report which was sent to Geneva and was edited and circulated as a United Nations document?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Z942 is the exhibit for production, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I propose to do, this document being available to the Defence, is to get him to tell you himself what his conclusions are, and the document's a work of reference available as helpful. It's in English and French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, what were your conclusions as to which troops were involved in the attack?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our conclusion was that members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A very brief objection, Your Honour, and that is this: The report that Mr. Akhavan authored or participated in authoring says what it says. Any conclusions that he has are presumably articulated in that, and so I object to this testimony on that grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to me that that's a ground of objection. If the document already appears, the witness can refer to it and expand on it if he wish it. Perhaps you could refer to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The witness can refer to the report, paragraph 38 onwards, and expand on it if required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have in front of you paragraphs 38 and onwards. The easiest way is simply for you to read those reports, and I'll ask you for any expansion to those conclusions, 38 to 44. I'll ask for further amplification, possibly, of one or two points.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you like me to read --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just read it out. That's what's required now.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: "The information gathered in the preparation of this report demonstrates that the recent eruption of hostilities between Croat and government forces in central Bosnia and Herzegovina involved massive and systematic violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. "The forced displacement and detention of civilians" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please. Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, could you remember the interpreters, please, and slow down.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: "The forced displacement and detention of civilians, arbitrary executions, attacks on towns as well as the destruction of villages and religious sites have become part of a deliberate and systematic policy of ethnic cleansing conducted by Croat forces in that region. The fate of the civilian population of Ahmici is a particularly shocking application of this policy. "Arbitrary executions and torture have been carried out by government forces. The danger of retaliation for ethnic cleansing committed by Croat forces against Croat civilians in towns such as Zenica is a real one. "The credibility of the parties' commitment to human rights will be tested by their willingness to bring to justice the perpetrators of such atrocities as are outlined in this report. "Commitments which all parties to the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina have repeatedly entered into to respect human rights and international humanitarian law, including written agreements concluded upon international mediation, have been systematically violated. "The peace plan, according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina would be divided along ethnic lines, has been used in order to create ethnically homogeneous areas. The lack of an effective international response to counter the policy of ethnic cleansing perpetrated by Serb forces from the beginning of the war created the precedent of impunity which has allowed them to continue and which has encouraged Croat forces to adopt the same policy. "Without stopping the war and without applying sufficient pressure to force an end to human rights violations any attempts to find a just and lasting political solution will be doomed to fail."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were your overall conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could you ask the witness, Mr. Akhavan, whether his conclusions, Item 43, in which he talks about the peace plan, whether this means the Vance-Owen Plan, or which peace plan?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it refers to the Vance-Owen Plan. But I should explain that these are not my personal conclusions. These are the conclusions of the United Nations Special Rapporteur, Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, who was the former prime minister of Poland, and of course the conclusions are based in large part upon the information and analysis which we had supplied to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your conclusions, in relation specifically to Ahmici, say what, as to the forces who had conducted the atrocity?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was clear from virtually every source of testimony and evidence that we had that it was overwhelmingly HVO forces that were responsible for the atrocities in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number of soldiers, the quantity of artillery, and to the degree you were able to assess it, the amount of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once again, based on the assistance of military experts and our own investigation of the area, it was clear that the attack involved a significant amount of military resources. It was hardly an attack perpetrated by a group of rogue elements. According to what we gathered, there must have been approximately 100, 150 soldiers involved in the operation -- a company, according to members of the British Battalion who accompanied us -- and it was clear that a wide range of weapons, including mortars, including guns of various sorts, including rocket-propelled grenades, including also the use of incendiary devices, the use of petrol to burn homes, that there was a significant coordination and use of resources in the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to offer, on the basis of the information coming to you, any opinion on the amount of ammunition, by numbering the rounds and so on?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we estimated that several thousand rounds would have been used, based simply on the number of spent shells which we could see around each of the homes and making some sort of estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, just help us with this: How near to or far from the village of Ahmici were the HVO commanders at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I recall, the HVO headquarters of Mr. Blaskic were maybe just a couple of kilometres down the road from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that feature in your considerations at all?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the factors that we considered in assessing whether Mr. Blaskic, as well as others in the HVO leadership, would have been aware that there was a military operation on a large scale taking place in Ahmici over several hours in one day. To us, it added to the implausibility of their claim that they may not have been aware that such an operation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the question of the village of Miletici, what view, if any, did you form or do you hold about the attack on that village and its comparison with what you saw at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in a sincere effort to be evenhanded in our investigations, we would always try and see whether there were violations committed by other parties to the conflict as well. The village of Miletici, as the report explains, involves a group of, apparently, members of the so-called Mujahedin, which were often a mixture of outside mercenaries and locals, who had beheaded some young Croatian men. Our assessment of that atrocity was that it was probably perpetrated on a small scale. It was not the result of a large-scale, organised operation involving significant resources. It was a handful of men who had come to a hamlet where most of the people were elderly, and they had simply taken out the three or four young men of military age, had tortured and killed them. We clearly indicated in our report that the Bosnian government similarly should investigate this matter, but there was no indication whatsoever that this was part of a widespread or systematic policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you give any particular consideration to the possible connection of the Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Brigade in relation to this topic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had heard from several people that the so-called Mujahedin were actually operating alongside the Bosnian army; others suggested that they were simply rogue elements who answered to nobody and that they were quite independent of the Bosnian government. For the purposes of this particular investigation, it was very clear to us that Miletici was very much an isolated event in the Lasva Valley region, and we did not really get into what the formal association was of the Mujahedin with the regular army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your report draw criticism?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it did, from the authorities of Herceg-Bosna, which was the Bosnian Croat entity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that criticism verbal, or in the form of a letter?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the form of a letter sent to Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that letter? We haven't been able to produce it yet, but do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have a copy, not with me at present, but I have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you could find that in your office, perhaps at the break --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- if we asked you? Summarise its effect.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the report basically -- the letter basically suggested that our report had been one-sided; that it unfairly accused the Bosnian Croats of having committed atrocities, whereas, in reality, the Bosnian Muslims were largely responsible for atrocities in the region. It suggested that the investigators of Mr. Mazowiecki, for one reason or another, were not impartial, and it proceeded to mention two or three details which were not accurate in order to challenge the credibility of the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may be in a position to look at the letter a little later today, but did the content of the letter cause you to displace to any degree the conclusions you had already reached?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not really. I don't think that the letter provided any satisfactory explanation as to why we should not conclude that there had been massive violations of human rights in the affected areas and why we should not believe the overwhelming testimony to the effect that the HVO was responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO take steps to investigate these crimes, to your knowledge, or not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any suggestions or indications that they did?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a discussion, after the events in Ahmici, there were some discussions facilitated by the European Community Monitoring Mission between the Bosnian government and Bosnian Croat forces to have some sort of commission which would inquire into the matter. But as far as I know, no such investigation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had such an investigation taken place and a report been prepared, would you have expected the report to be forwarded to the United Nations, in light of the report that you had filed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that if the authorities could send a letter of complaint to Mr. Mazowiecki concerning the impartiality of our report, that they could equally have sent us the results of an investigation, and I'm quite sure that the results of that investigation would have been reflected in future reports to the Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No such report was ever received?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role, on the basis of your experience, did Dario Kordic occupy in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Formerly speaking, he had explained to me and others had explained to me that he was vice-president of the HDZ and HVO in the Lasva Valley region, and, in fact, he appeared to be the most powerful and influential figure in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Deal, if you will, with his relationship to Boban and to Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can speak about his relation to Blaskic; I'm not very sure about his relation to Boban. My impression was that he was clearly in a position of authority vis-a-vis Mr. Blaskic. My impression, based on discussions I had with Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Kordic, based on discussions I had with members of the British Battalion and other sources in the region, was that Mr. Kordic was, so to say, the mastermind of HDZ/HVO policies in the region, and Mr. Blaskic was, if you like, the executor of those policies. That, in a general way, is how I would describe the relationship. I had heard that Mr. Kordic occupied a prominent place in the Herceg-Bosna political establishment and that he was -- had enjoyed a close relationship with Mate Boban. But as I said, I had no opportunities to observe that personally, so that was just my general impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The line of demarcation between military and political authority, how easy was that to be drawn in the circumstances where you found yourself?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My impression is that it was extremely difficult to separate the two, that the HDZ/HVO structures were very tightly integrated and that there was very little distinction between military and civilian structures of authority and command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask, save just to confirm that the filing system in your office, is it such that within 20 minutes or half an hour, when we have a break, you will be able to locate that letter and have it copied for Defence and everyone else, if they haven't got a copy already?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just check on the known position of the other witness? So far as the other witness is concerned, Your Honour, he is, I gather, on the plane. It's not known what his reaction to staying the night is, but, of course, providing he can get up early tomorrow morning, it's always possible he could go back, if that's necessary, and return again tomorrow. I will keep the Chamber posted as to events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I believe that you were one of the prosecutors who argued before the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in the Drazen Erdemovic case?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually appeared as the prosecutor in that appeal, I believe?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you may have authored an article that appeared last year in the American University International Law Review?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read to you a portion of that and see if you agree with this. You said that the Erdemovic case was actually the first case that had been argued before the Appeals Chamber; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that you made this observation in the course of your article: "Of course, the Prosecution tried to argue (and I am going to speak in the third person in order to avoid implicating myself)"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you have given two prior statements to the office for which you work, the Office of the Prosecution, one dated December 13th, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it was with respect to investigations generally, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a statement that you yourself authored; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you gave another statement dated June the 23rd, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date of these statements. One was a statement that I myself authored; another should be a statement which was written by one of our investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You actually signed that statement two years after the interview, I believe, in 1997, just before the Blaskic trial; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I signed it two years after the fact. It could be that I signed it at that time, having read the statements and having found that it accurately reflected what I had written in my own statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you testified in the Blaskic case in December of 1997. In fact, you testified, I believe, on December the 15th, 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was two months after the Erdemovic judgement was handed down by the Appeals Chamber. You also testified for two days in Kupreskic on August the 27th and the 31st, 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you do agree, I believe, that your investigations on behalf of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights occurred during the midst of a complex civil war between various ethnic factions in the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Croats occasionally were locked in battle with the Serbs and forces from the former JNA located in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And occasionally, the Muslims and Croats would fall to fighting amongst one another as well?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A complex and confusing situation, I think you would agree?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In certain respects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you when you went to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Six years ago would take me to 27 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twenty-seven years old. When were you first hired by the United Nations Centre for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was hired one year prior to that. It was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever done any work on this case, apart from your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start working as a legal assistant for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I started working as a legal advisor to the Prosecution in April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been working as a legal advisor for the Prosecution for the last five years?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And occasionally arguing cases on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, one appellate case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually argued some motions in the Blaskic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not argue them but I drafted them for the Prosecution, and they were all motions dealing with doctrinal issues, not with factual issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a few questions, if I might, regarding your experience, qualifications, and background. You gave testimony about having graduated from Osgoode Hall Law School at the University of Toronto.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's actually at York University in Toronto, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you graduate with that degree, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you also informed the Trial Chamber that you now have a law degree from the Harvard Law School, I believe?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you obtain that degree?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In 1990, the following year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever practised as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not, not in -- I've never been a member of a national bar, but I've practised as a lawyer in this jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your graduation from Harvard Law School, where did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I worked in a human rights non-governmental organisation in Geneva, Switzerland which dealt with U.N. human rights system in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The organisation was called the Bahai International Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work for the Bahai International Community?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a three-month period on a pro bono basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that three-month period, where did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: After that, I worked at the Norwegian Institute of Human Rights in Oslo for a U.N. expert dealing with ethnic conflicts in what was then the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would have been in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This would have been in 1990 still, September of 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the summer after law school, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any kind of military background at all?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ever served in the armed forces of any country?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever fired a weapon?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever stripped or cleaned a weapon?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any police background?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been trained in any way in investigative or forensic techniques?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were trained in investigative techniques prior not only to my work with the United Nations Centre for Human Rights, but also in connection with two international missions that I participated in prior to joining the U.N.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that training?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The training was given in one case by the United Nations itself, in another case, because it was a diplomatic mission, various foreign ministries that we were involved in provided us with assistance with training, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this training last?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The training in the case of the missions would always be a couple of days prior to the actual mission. In the case of the U.N. Centre for Human Rights, there was ongoing training, as well as the initial period of training, prior to being deployed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been given any systematic, organised, detailed training in the performance of a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because we were not conducting criminal investigations. We were conducting human rights investigations, which are very different in nature than criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any familiarity with the concept of giving warnings about constitutional or legal rights?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have a familiarity with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the context of a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the context of a criminal investigation, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any recitations of those rights given to Colonel Blaskic, Mario Cerkez, or Dario Kordic before you met them in early May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because the investigations were not in the nature of criminal investigations. There was no international criminal court in place at that time even, so it seemed totally irrelevant at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, isn't it true that the Security Council resolution establishing the International Criminal Tribunal was passed on February the 22nd of 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not strictly speaking. It was on May 25th, 1993 that resolution 827 was adopted. Resolution 808, to which you refer, was simply the expression of an intent on the part of the Security Council to look into the establishment of a court, when, for that purpose, the Secretary-General was asked to prepare a report. The report which came out with respect to Ahmici is dated 19 May, 1993, actually just one week prior to the establishment of this court, and the investigation itself had taken place even earlier. So I don't think that the prospect of criminal investigations was at all in the forefront of any of our minds when we were engaging in preparing this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Colonel Blaskic, Mr. Cerkez, or Mr. Kordic that they didn't have to say anything at all to you, but that if they did, it could certainly be taken down and used in evidence against them?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once again, that was not at all in issue. The investigation was not against any of those individuals. A human rights report concerns itself with state responsibility, and in the context of a complex armed conflict, to which you yourself referred, one looks at which are the parties which are in de facto control of a particular territory and which actually exercise governmental powers. Our interest was in affording Mr. Kordic, Blaskic, and Cerkez an opportunity to counter the testimony of members of the British Battalion, of the survivors of Ahmici, along the lines of the audi alteram partem rule, to allow both sides to give their side of the story. There was absolutely no obligation on their part to say anything to us, I think that was very clear, and it was simply an opportunity for them to give us their side of the story so that we could write, to the extent possible, an impartial report. I don't think at any point that the issue of their individual criminal liability was really at the forefront of our meetings. But we did, as part of the general mandate of the human rights special rapporteur to encourage authorities to comply with human rights standard, suggest to them that they should, indeed, they are responsible for conducting investigations and for bringing the perpetrators to justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the testimony that you have just given this morning about Mr. Cerkez, for example, I believe that you told the Trial Chamber that Mr. Cerkez was informed by yourself and also by Colonel Stewart that if he did not perform some sort of an investigation, then he would be held liable; isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, correct, but we did not suggest that we would be the agency conducting an investigation and holding him liable. We simply said that under international law, that he is responsible and that he must take that responsibility seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn briefly to the statements that you have given to the Prosecution. The first one, the December the 13th, 1994 statement, is actually written in your own words; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with the investigators in 1995, you were asked to relate accurately what the people you had interviewed had told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you did not even read your June the 23rd, 1995 statement until mid December of 1997?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the statement -- the report which the investigators made of the interview with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall what the situation was at that time, but I do recall having eventually reviewed it and having asked the Prosecutor to clarify one or two points which were somewhat ambiguous during the testimony of the Blaskic trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually stated, I believe, under oath that the June the 23rd, 1995 statement was not, strictly speaking, your statement but a statement that was taken from you by two investigators; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that there were some inaccuracies in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there were ambiguities which were resolved at trial through explanations which I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that there was a significant distortion in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Page 5364.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- concerning the contention that Colonel Blaskic would not have the intelligence to plan the offensive operations in the Lasva Valley but that Mr. Kordic would have the knowledge; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I'm not sure that "significant distortion" would be the appropriate term. I think that I objected to the way that sentence was formulated in order to be respectful towards the accused in that case, Mr. Blaskic, and I think the point was not that he did not have the intelligence but that he was not the mastermind, if you like, of the policy of the HDZ and HVO in the region in the same way that Mr. Kordic was. That was the point that I was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic tell you that Mr. Kordic was the mastermind in the area? He didn't, did he?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Cerkez didn't tell you that either, did he, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in those terms. I think both of them conceded that Mr. Kordic was the highest ranking authority in the region, but the idea of Mr. Kordic being the mastermind, so to speak, was largely the result of both my own observations and of what I'd been told by members of various international organisations which were present in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe that you arrived in Zagreb towards the end of April 1993 to take up your work on behalf of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you best recall, I believe, it was the European Community Monitoring Mission that actually came to you concerning the need for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: While we were looking into the matter, there were obviously in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time a large number of violations which one could have investigated, and it must be recalled that Ahmici occurred --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, the question was simple. Was it or was it not the ECMM that came to you to ask you to get involved in an investigation?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not the cause for the investigation. We had considered investigating the matter, as I was trying to explain, among a wide range of violations which had been brought to our attention, and the meeting with the ECMM, of course, persuaded us to give priority to that investigation. But they, of course, did not decide for us what we would investigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ECMM tell you that it was actually dispatching its own deputation to do precisely what you proposed to do?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We knew that the ECMM had an office in the field in the region of Central Bosnia. I don't remember whether this was specifically discussed, but the ECMM did believe that the United Nations would be the most appropriate body to conduct the investigation. When we were in the field, yes, we did cooperate with ECMM representatives, and we were aware that they were conducting a similar investigation, although I think the nature of their investigation was somewhat different than ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think they dealt with broader security issues, which we would not have concerned ourselves with, and their investigator, as I recall, was, indeed, a military man who dealt not only with -- or not even primarily with the atrocities but with their security implications for the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, as you prepared yourself to perform this investigation that you've described, did you have access to any written materials that described recent events in the Lasva Valley involving interethnic violence between Croat factions and Muslim factions?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Any written material?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: On occasion we would have access to what are called sitreps, situation reports, or other summaries which were provided through the U.N. Protection Force chain of command, reporting on the situation in the region. We had, I think, a very general sense about the security situation in the region, but we didn't concern ourselves too much with that. The point of our investigation was to look at violations of humanitarian law which had occurred and to try and prioritise those which had been committed on a widespread or massive scale. We were aware that breaches of ceasefire and other security-related matters were very complex and that they were only relevant in a tangential sense to our mandate, which was to look at human rights violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if the witness might be shown Exhibit D25/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, I wonder, have you seen this document before, the document entitled "Special Report on Croats in Zenica, 20 to 21st of April, 1993"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, since this goes back to some six years, I don't recall whether we had visited this specific document. But I do recognise the subject matter, which is reflected more or less in the report of May 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that significant numbers of Croat civilians had been killed in the villages mentioned in paragraph 2, the Croat communities in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We were not aware of those specific villages, but we did indicate in our report that, as was the case with Miletici, that there were isolated attacks against Croats. And I think the report which I read out specifically did indicate that the situation in Zenica is very tense and that there is a fear of retaliation. So in answer to your question, those specific villages which are indicated in this report may not have been mentioned, in part because we were not in a position, with limited time and resources, to visit everywhere, but we did, I think, reflect the fact that the Croats in Zenica were in a difficult situation. But in our opinion, there was nothing approximating the scale of killings and atrocities which had been committed against the Muslims. In order to put forward a balanced report, I believe that we had to concentrate more of our attention and resources on situations such as that of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the massacres of Croat civilians at the villages of Dusina, Lasva, Nezirovici, and Gusti Grab on January the 26th, 1993, sir? Anything?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was not even in the employ of the United Nations Centre for Human Rights at that time, so I would not have been involved in such an investigation. But as I said, our reports are not about who shot whom first; our reports are objective accounts of violations which we believe happened to be particularly serious. Obviously, throughout the war, there were all sorts of atrocities committed by all sides, and it was virtually impossible, with a small staff, to investigate each and every atrocity, which is why we concentrated on those situations which we thought were particularly flagrant, and we believed that Ahmici and environs did clearly fall into the category of particularly serious offences. Nonetheless, we did make the effort, to the best of our ability, to reflect the fact that Bosnian Muslims had also committed atrocities against Bosnian Croats, but by no objective standard could we see any form of equivalence between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were travelling throughout the Lasva Valley, did you realise that hundreds of Croat civilians were being held, imprisoned, in the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did receive reports that people were being imprisoned, but we did not receive reports that they were being particularly seriously mistreated. We did not receive any credible reports, for example, of executions of these people, nor that they were being held in concentration-camp conditions, for example. And I think the report which you yourself have produced also testifies that they were generally well treated in prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, apart from the 30 that showed signs of brutality?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the 30 that showed signs of brutality?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which 30? I'm sorry, I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at the first paragraph of Exhibit D25/1, I think you'll see it there. Quote: "About 30 showed signs of brutality."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. No, this is true. You see, this is all relative to the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, as I said. I would be surprised indeed if, in most of these situations, there would not be brutality. This was a brutal war, and as I explained, virtually all sides were engaged in various degrees of what we would consider, in objective terms, violations of international humanitarian law. But still, in terms of where we would prioritise resources, the case of 30 prisoners who may have, for example, been beaten or treated with brutality, was simply not the same as the killing of 100 to 200 men, women, and children in the village of Ahmici, not to mention Vitez and other surrounding villages. So we would, instead of spending two days investigating the brutalities against 30 inmates, make a sentence in a general sense in our report, as we have, that the situation of Croats in Zenica is difficult and perilous, but we would not spend the same amount of time and energy investigating this as we would have investigating the atrocities in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you were in Central Bosnia for six days performing your investigations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: One week, probably, from April 30th to May the 6th. Seven days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Seven days; I'm sorry. Now, it would be fair to say that all sides in this civil war, in your experience, regularly accused each other of having committed atrocities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was, if you like, a standard defensive technique?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was part of the propaganda war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you finished with the exhibit, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning for a minute to the ECMM mission that was visiting Central Bosnia simultaneously with you and your colleague, did you ever speak to Jeremy Fleming?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I met several people from the ECMM; I wouldn't remember the names of any of them except Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that a joint body for the investigation of incidents and other items, called the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission, had been formed?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember being informed during our first meeting with the ECMM that they had mediated between the Bosnian Croats and Muslims and had created some sort of investigative body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Croat representatives sat on that body, sir, what their identity was?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one ever told you that Dario Kordic sat on the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission in any capacity, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wouldn't surprise me if that were the case, but to us, these investigative commissions very often were quite empty, and they never really amounted to anything. So we had, in many cases, even dealing with Bosnian Serbs, all sorts of commissions which were entrusted with investigating atrocities, and even in the face of overwhelming atrocities, they very rarely, if ever, resulted in a serious investigation or serious prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To return to my question, no one ever told you that Mr. Kordic sat on the Busovaca Joint Coordination Commission or had any connection with it, did they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I do recall, though, we met the establishment of this commission with understandable scepticism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you know that Colonel Stewart sat on the coordination committee, this commission?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do recall that he was involved in some capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: But all of these, I think, transpired after our mission was completed. I believe that the commission was, as far as I remember, not yet formally constituted, in the sense that it was not yet engaging in its activities, or had just begun to do so, when we had arrived there. Because we had arrived there quite soon after the acts had occurred in Ahmici and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown Exhibit D23/1, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, have you ever seen Exhibit D23/1 before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not. I believe that I may actually have been mistaken. The commission which the ECMM had informed us about was probably not this, but another commission specifically established to look into the events in the Lasva Valley region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would turn to the third page, the organisational structure of the joint coordination committee is explained. We have the commanding officer of BritBat, and that was Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart; right? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Was the commanding officer of the BritBat -- yes, it was Colonel Stewart at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the ECMM chairman, and that was Jeremy Fleming; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the commander of the BiH 3rd Corps; do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but I had, I believe, even met this gentleman. But I don't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I mention the name General Enver Hadzihasanovic, would that be someone that you've met before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, have you met General Enver Hadzihasanovic before, or have you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe I did during my stay there. To the best of my recollection, after six years, yes, I did meet a number of military personnel from the Bosnian army as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would consulting your notes help you to remember who you saw and what they said?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall actually having an interview with any of these people. We were at the UNPROFOR compound for one week, and there was regular traffic of both Bosnian army and HVO personnel and a number of others in that area, so I do recall that we had met members of the Bosnian army who had come to discuss with UNPROFOR, ECMM, the ICRC, several other organisations which were situated there. But I actually don't recall having had any sort of interview with them, because we didn't think it was relevant to what we were investigating at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get on to the subject of your notes, let me just ask you: Who was the commander of the HVO central command?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The commander, in military terms, I believe, was Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander in chief of the HVO armed forces was at this time?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall. It could have been Petkovic, but I really don't remember at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you made notes contemporaneously as you visited various people and travelled around the Lasva Valley during your one-week visit at the end of April and May of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I took notes where it was relevant to the matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you put down who said what to whom; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: When it was relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a note of who you met?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made notes of what you were told by the people that you met?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've lost those notes, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Those notes have been recovered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are copies of the notes in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the notes that you have are downstairs?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Upstairs, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upstairs. Have you consulted those notes, sir, in preparing for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in preparation for the testimony today. I've consulted them, I would say, three or four weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if we might consult those notes over the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you can retrieve them during the lunch break and they could be handed over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any tape recordings, Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At this point, Mr. President, I think we need to go into a private session just for about 30 seconds, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the witness was here, there are a couple of questions that Mr. Lopez-Terres needed to ask that haven't been asked because the Victims and Witnesses Unit didn't tell him that the witness had arrived. Another ten minutes is proposed. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, have you got something you can deal with for ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. I don't think we need to detain Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you if you would like to ask him some more things, since he's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It might be appropriate, Your Honour, to go back into private session, since we're dealing with a confidential witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Akhavan, from the slits in the tank that you were driving through Ahmici in on May the 1st, 1993, you could actually see men looting houses; could you not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the slits in the tank"? We actually were -- the tanks actually had a roof in the passenger compartment where we could actually stand up outside of the tank and observe. But, yes, we did see people looting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not tell which side those people belonged to, could you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I could simply tell that they wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know what the disposition of the front lines between the Croat forces and Muslim forces on May the 1st, 1993 was, do you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a general sense, perhaps no, but we did know specifically that Ahmici was under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive information from your military briefers that the HVO, as of April the 30th, 1993, was on the verge of a crushing military defeat in the entire Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, we were not given any such indication, and even at the admission of Colonel Blaskic, the HVO was in firm control of the Lasva Valley region, including Ahmici, which we specifically discussed. I don't recall Mr. Kordic either telling me at any point that they were under a threat of imminent defeat from the Bosnian Muslims. No one, as a matter of fact, said that to me. I am aware that sometime after the campaign of ethnic cleansing in Ahmici and environs, that there was a Bosnian Muslim counteroffensive. My understanding at that time was that most of the Bosnian Muslim army was caught up in trying to fight against Bosnian Serbs and that they did not have a significant amount of resources positioned against the Bosnian Croats. That situation may have changed after the events in the Lasva Valley, and I believe our reports of May the 19th actually foresaw such a possibility. And, of course, our concern being one of violations of humanitarian law, we did express our concern in that report, that if justice is not done, if there is not some form of accountability for the events, that, indeed, there may be some sort of retaliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, when you get to a convenient moment. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This moment is as good as any, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Akhavan, thank you very much. Would you be back, please, when you are asked to conclude your evidence? Hopefully this week. Meanwhile, would you perhaps get the copies of the notes and hand them to the Prosecutors for onward transmission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: May we also request a copy of the letter to which the witness referred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The letter from Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the letter from Herceg-Bosna to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one, the one that was referred to by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not have a copy of that letter in my own files. I will try and find it, but I'm not in a position to promise that I can do so in the short span of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if you can find it. Thank you. If you would like to go now. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres will call the next witness. I understand he is willing to stay overnight, but because of the other witnesses who we want accommodate, we will, nevertheless, try and take him as quickly in chief as we can. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Andrew Williams, born on the 31st of May, 1958?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You joined the British army in May 1976 and you left in May 1998, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are now an owner of a pub in Manchester?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were Colour Sergeant in the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Bosnia, you served as an intelligence officer in your regiment from November 1992 until May 1993, and you were stationed in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the framework of your duties, you moved around yourself, and daily, directly or through the soldiers of your company, you received information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information was then conveyed to your officers, first Major Rule and then Major Jones, who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your area of responsibility covered the municipalities of Bugojno in the north, Prozor in the south, and Gornji Vakuf in the centre?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.
