utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you yourself collected this information, either directly or from your soldiers, you drafted daily reports which were addressed to your headquarters in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those reports were then summarised in Vitez and distributed under the name of "milinfosum"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, the town of Gornji Vakuf, in which you were stationed, was it situated on an important road, a communication line?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a very important road for both us and the local militias. It was one of the few access routes from the border up into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a former military man, would you say that that town had a special strategic interest in view of its position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have a very special strategic position because whoever controlled the town would control the route and, therefore, would control one of the entry routes into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The majority of the population of Gornji Vakuf were of Muslim ethnicity, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Gornji Vakuf with your company, what was the character and quality of the relationship that you were able to see between the two communities, the Croats and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were united in that they had a common enemy, the Bosnian Serbs, but there was a great deal of mistrust between the two sides. They did not like each other and didn't trust each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I'm going to show you a document. It is a document on which you will see most of the localities that we have mentioned and particularly the one we will ask you to comment on during your testimony. It is Exhibit Z2612/6. Do you see the document on your screen, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us, with the help of the pointer that you have on the table, could you show us the localities of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is the town of Bugojno (indicating) at the top there. In the centre here is the town of Gornji Vakuf (indicating) or Gornja Vakuf. In the south here is the town of Prozor (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you will be asked to talk about the Makljen pass, the villages of Bistrica, Hrasnica. Could you show us these localities on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Hrasnica area is here (indicating), Bistrica is a small village just outside Gornji Vakuf here (indicating), and the Makljen was a checkpoint on top of the high feature just to the north of Prozor here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will also be speaking about three other localities, that is, Uzricje, Dusa, and Rumboci. Could you show them on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first two villages are here and Rumboci is down here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, I'm going to show you another document. It is a document issued in January 1996 showing the borders of the various cantons as envisaged by the Vance-Owen Plan at the time. This is document Z2582. Mr. Williams, you have that document before you. As far as you know, the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, was it supposed to go under the Croatian administration, according to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. When they drew the lines on the map, Canton 10, which covered this sort of northern Herzegovina and Central Bosnia area, was supposed to become a Croat-controlled canton or a Bosnian Croat-controlled canton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The provisions of this plan, the Vance-Owen Plan, how were they received by the Muslim community at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were not very happy about the fact that they were going to be placed under Croat control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim population of the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, and you said that they were in the majority, did they see their ranks increase as a result of the influx of refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of refugees in the Gornji Vakuf area that had come from a town called Jajce, I can't pronounce it properly, a town called Jajce or something, which is just to the northwest of Travnik, and also from another town called Gornji Vakuf, which is the other side of Bugojno, both of which, Jajce and Gornji Vakuf, had fallen to the Serbs, and a Muslim population had moved into the Muslim area of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information that you were able to collect at the time, what was the reaction of the Croats of Gornji Vakuf in relation to those refugees? Did they welcome them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They wanted the Muslim refugees to be moved further into Central Bosnia, into the Zenica area, because they felt that the ethnic balance had shifted too far in favour of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The usher may return to his seat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, in the course of your tour of duty, you registered a number of incidents which heightened tension between the two communities.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Tribunal has already learned about some of those incidents, so we will cover them very quickly, some of them at least. Do you remember one particular incident which involved the beheading of a Muslim by an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This murder, did it worsen relations between the two communities of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Very much so. It also damaged the relations between ourselves and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed of the return of the perpetrator of this crime to the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When the fighting erupted in Gornji Vakuf between the Croats and the Muslims, one of the problems we had, as we were trying to broker ceasefires, was to get both sides to trust each other. One of the reasons that the Muslims would not trust the Croats was because when the incident happened, the beheading, the soldier concerned, the Muslims wanted him tried in one of their courts, and the Bosnian Croats instead tried him in Mostar. As the fighting erupted in Gornji Vakuf, that soldier returned and took part in the fighting, and as a result, the Muslims felt that they could not trust what the Croats said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also recall, Mr. Williams, that around December 1992 or January 1993, a former school, which was supposed to be used by the two armies, was taken by a group of soldiers belonging to the HOS in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a small detachment of HOS who lived in one of the small schools. They took control -- it was a joint billet, and they cleared out the Muslim soldiers that were sharing it with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about this HOS group which took control of the building? Do you have information about that group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were only a small group, somewhere around about a dozen to fifteen of them, one of which was a woman and a couple of which were mercenaries. They did not figure largely in anything in Gornji Vakuf, and they just disappeared. They either moved out or were absorbed into the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned mercenaries. Were there one or several mercenaries of British origin?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was at least one British mercenary in the HOS, and there was also a British mercenary -- at least one British mercenary in the HVO, who I actually used to speak to and used to get information from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This British mercenary which could have belonged to the HOS, did you discover his identity, his name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The mercenary that I used to use, who I used -- who I knew his name properly, was in the HVO. The one that was in the HOS, I'm not 100 per cent certain of his name, other than he was, I believe, a former tank soldier in the British army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name "Chris Kenneth Wilson" say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is probably the name of the mercenary that was in the HOS who was the former tank soldier. The other mercenary, that I used to speak to properly, that I used to use as a source, was also a former British soldier, but he was in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to that second mercenary a little later in the course of your testimony. At the time that we are now talking about, you were informed, through your meetings with responsible persons from the HVO, that they intended to establish law and order in the region of Gornji Vakuf, participants and that in that context, they were charged with the protection of the Muslims by the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In theory, if the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had gone ahead, yes, that would have been correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the same period. Did you note that the HVO soldiers in the region for which you were responsible started stopping all vehicles bearing license plates from Bosnia and asking the owners of these vehicles to have new license plates posted carrying the flag of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: At about the same period of time, there was some agitation that -- that the Bosnian Croats wished to form their own state of Herceg-Bosna. In the areas in which they had control, or believed they had control, they started to try to make the population change the license plates of their cars to a license plate that bore the shield of Herceg-Bosna in the centre of it. They also instituted, at such places as the Makljen checkpoint, that you could not go through the checkpoint without a visa, and the only place you could get the visa was from a HVO office, and you had to buy it. So in effect, it was a form of tax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January 1993, the conflict escalated and became much more serious in Gornji Vakuf; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your soldiers noted that HVO forces coming from several other municipalities in the region, and which were placed under the command of Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, asserted themselves in the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As the fighting escalated in Gornji Vakuf, a lot of external forces from the HVO were brought into the area and used to seal the town. Would you like me to name the brigades?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you can remember, we would be glad for to you to list them.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were units or subunits from the Tomislav Brigade; there were subunits from the Prva Ramska Brigade, which was the Prozor HVO. There were subunits from the Petar Kresimir or Kresimo (phoen) Brigade, which came from Livno or Duvno, just the other side of Tomislavgrad. There were subunits from Mostar. Some of the Bugojno HVO moved down the road to seal the road between Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, and there were also external troops from a brigade called the Bruno Busic Brigade, although the Bruno Busic Brigade did have a small detachment present in Gornji Vakuf anyway. And there were also troops -- I can't remember the names of the brigades, but there were troops from a town called Grude and troops from another town not far from Grude. At one time during the fighting we actually managed to have a ceasefire where each side agreed to have liaison officers from the other side placed on their gun lines in places like that. When the fighting restarted, we got back one of the Muslim soldiers who was put on an HVO gun line as a monitoring officer, and he said -- when we asked him how many HVO soldiers he'd actually seen, his reply was, "The whole of Herzegovina is out there." Which obviously was an exaggeration, but we took that to confirm that there were units from all across northwest Herzegovina present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just speaking of a meeting that was organised to try and appease the conflict between the two parties and to achieve a ceasefire. Could you indicate who were the participants in those meetings, one or several?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were several meetings. It became a bit -- us trying to negotiate ceasefires and both sides agreeing to ceasefires became a bit of a standing joke. In the end, we stopped calling them "ceasefires"; we called them "periods of calm" instead. There were delegates -- at various meetings taking place, there were delegates from Mostar, delegates from Zenica. On our side, initially, it was my company commander, at times it was my commanding officer from Vitez, Colonel Stewart, and at times -- on one of the meetings, it was even General Morillon. The ECMM ambassador, Ambassador Bousseau, also took part in one meeting. There were delegates that came from the Red Cross who took part in some of the meetings. Names that spring to mind as being there on various meetings were a Bosnian army Muslim officer by the name of Merdan from Zenica; a major from the Bosnian army from the Corps headquarters, 3 Corps headquarters, called Selmo Cikotic, or Cikotak (phoen); a colonel from Mostar, from the HVO, called Colonel Andric, or something similar to Andric; Brigadier Petkovic; Colonel Siljeg; the local commanders from the two local Gornji Vakuf brigades, the HVO and the Armija Bosna. Zrinko Tokic was the commander of the HVO brigade in Gornji Vakuf. There were several meetings, and there were different delegates on each one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, among other people, you mentioned the name of a colonel from Mostar by the name of Andric.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you remember that he read a kind of an ultimatum to the Bosnian and Herzegovinian army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he did read -- he read an ultimatum which -- we had just spent several hours trying to negotiate a ceasefire, whereupon he produced this ultimatum, which was already pretyped on a piece of paper, which surprised us, because it meant to us that he had no intention of negotiating a settlement to this at all, or he wouldn't have had the ultimatum already prepared. The ultimatum was to the effect that Gornji Vakuf was, under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, to become part of a Croat-controlled opstina -- Croat-controlled canton, and that therefore they wished to take control of it. They wished the BH army to hand in their weapons. They wished the head of the Bosnian army brigade and the head of the Bosnian military police and the head of the Bosnian police to be detained and tried as war criminals. They wished all the external Muslim troops to be removed from the town. Anybody who did not want to be under Croat rule was to leave, and that they had two brigades formed up in Prozor ready to attack the town unless they agreed to those terms. They also wished the media to publish that all the incidents that had happened prior to this were the results of Muslim gangsters, and that the HVO were attempting to bring law and order to the municipality, and that they had not killed anybody, and they had not damaged any house and had not committed any other form of crime. This, of course, the Bosnian army or the Muslim Bosnian army were not going to agree to, and as a result, a major attack started on the town the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those negotiations held in Gornji Vakuf, did one of the negotiators on the Croat part, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, use your fax machine, the one that was installed in your office? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The office I worked from contained the only phone line that we had in our base, and it was an INMARSAT, satellite telephone, that was also connected to a fax. He used to make phone calls, and after he'd made the phone calls, I used to print out the numbers that he had dialled and pass the numbers up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you establish which ZIP code area, which area was he calling?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The area code for the phone numbers that he phoned would indicate that they were from Split, or the Split area. It was the Split area code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Split is in Croatia, isn't it, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also placed at the disposal of another Croat representative your own telephone; that is an INMARSAT telephone, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that other representative, was he General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: General Milivoj Petkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you establish, which area code was he dialling when he used your equipment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was the same area code. It was the Split area code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, when you answered the questions in May 1995 of one of our investigators, you gave us a sketch and organisation of the HVO forces in the region, and there was a sketch, an organisational diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is Z2763. This is a three-page document, and I'm referring to page 3 of the document. Subsequently, I shall go back to page 1 of the same document. Usher, could you please turn to page 3, which is an organisational diagram. Yes, this is the one; organisational chart, page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, do you recognise this document as the one that you handed over to the investigators in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, and could you explain to us, what was his function? Where was his place on this chart?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He commanded Op Zone Northwest Herzegovina, so he would be here. Op Zone Northwest Herzegovina consisted of these brigades and probably also other assets as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the names of a number of brigades which you remembered and which were at the basis of this organisational chart.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Do you mean the Northwest Herzegovina brigades?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The Petar Kresimir or Kresimo Brigade, something similar to that, Petar Kresimir or Kresimo from the Livno/Duvno area; the Tomislav Brigade, which was commanded by a Canadian national called Nick Glasnovic; the Prva Ramska or 1st Rama Brigade, which came from Prozor; the Ante Starcevic Brigade, which was commanded by Zrinko Tokic, which came from Gornji Vakuf; and the Bugojno Brigade, which was commanded by a gentleman called Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I should like to show you another document, which is Z2414. As you can see, this document was written in Tomislavgrad on the 12th of April, 1993, and it is from the command for the Northwest Operative Zone. It is signed by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, do you know if Colonel Zeljko Siljeg was the same one who took part in the Gornji Vakuf negotiations that we spoke about before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same Colonel Siljeg. We had a nickname for him. We used to call him "Colonel Eyebrows" because he had big, bushy eyebrows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already told us -- you told us about those two ceasefire agreements and the negotiations in January 1993 in Gornji Vakuf, and now I should like to show you two milinfosums. The first one is of the 22nd of January, and the second, of the 24th of January, 1993. They are documents Z3881 and Z3901. Mr. Williams, will you please look at page 3 of the report of the 22nd January, 1993. In the upper part, the paragraph about Gornji Vakuf, which is paragraph 4 of the report, can you read that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this report refer to the negotiations about the ceasefire that we mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it refers to one of the ceasefires, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now would you mind looking at the other report, of the 24th January, 1993, the first page. Does it also refer to the negotiations that you spoke about before and the ceasefire agreement which was signed? Paragraph 1, Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm looking at a different document here. The one I'm looking at is Z388,1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Z390. The first page.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. We have the correct document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two documents, therefore, talk about negotiations which took place at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, in the course of the hostilities in the Gornji Vakuf area, did you and your soldiers observe that several villagers in the village had been attacked and destroyed by the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this destruction appear to you as something systematically done?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- one village in particular was deliberately cleansed. There was no other word for it. All of it was deliberate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These villages that you have in mind are?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The two where the worst incidents took place were the village of Bistrica and the village of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the second village, Hrasnica, you observed that that village had been destroyed and attacked on several occasions by the military police; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was visited and systematically destroyed on three occasions. Each time it was destroyed more and more severely in order to prevent people from coming back, until eventually, on the third occasion, it was completely levelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true that before the village was razed to the ground, it was also dynamited?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On the first instance, they just forced the population out, burned the houses. On the second visit, they then dynamited the houses to stop people returning because people had started to come back. On the third visit, they actually bulldozed it and flattened it completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you had to write, to compile these reports, milinfosums, in which you described those attacks, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now want to show you two documents. One of them is a milinfosum of the 11th of January, 1993 and the 1st of February, 1993. These are documents Z385 for the first one and Z429 for the second one. Could you have a look at document Z385? It is page 3 that I'm looking at. I don't think that is the page. Do you see paragraph 5 of the document, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document report one of the attacks that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now look at this second document, Z429, page 2? Can you also confirm that this report concerns another attack on the village of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could you tell us, what part of the document are you referring to, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As to the first document, Z385, I'm referring to page 3, paragraph 5. It concerns the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, and it says there that the HVO forces destroyed the predominantly Muslim village of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The second one is the document of the 1st of February, 1993, page 2. It is document Z429. So on page 2, there are two paragraphs. At the end of the second paragraph, it says that there was extensive damage to many Muslim villages, including the almost total destruction of the village of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, you have already mentioned another locality, and that is the locality of Bistrica, and you explained to us that artillery hit that particular Muslim village; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a BM-21-type multi-barreled rocket launcher which fired a full salvo of rockets onto the village. The rockets contained bomblets called KB-2 bomblets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, where did this artillery fire come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It came from near the village of Rumboci, just outside Prozor. Major Jones, who was my commanding officer at the time, was actually stood near to the multi-barreled rocket launcher when it fired, and he got back to the base and he said, "You won't believe what I've just seen. I've just seen a multi-barreled rocket launcher fire a full salvo," and we said, "Yes, we know. It's just landed on the village behind the base."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, when you find a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, I should merely like to show the witness two documents referring to that village, the village of Bistrica. They are milinfosums of the 23rd of January, 1993, Z388, and milinfosum 417 of the 29th of January, Z417. So the two documents I want to show are Z388 and Z417, it's a new document, Z388 and Z417.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, will you please look at the first document, Z388, page 2, the last part on page 2? It is a paragraph which speaks about the village of Bistrica, and is it referring to the fact that you just mentioned to us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it's referring to the multi-barreled rocket launcher attack on the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at the second document, Z417, page 4. You can't see the number 4, but it is the fourth page. Can you see at the end of it, paragraph 5, "Gornji Vakuf," and it again relates to the village of Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it does refer to the village of Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I believe that I have finished for the morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until 2.35. Mr. Williams, could you remember, during this and any other adjournments, maybe not to speak to anybody else about your evidence? That does include the members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are, in fact, going to move. It's already getting warm here. So we will move to Courtroom 2, where we will remain for the rest of the week. Perhaps somebody could direct the witness. Very well. At 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.06 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, this morning you told us before we broke for the break that you had information on the attack on the villages of Bistrica and Hrasnica. I should now like to ask you to tell us about other villages that were attacked, that is, the villages of Uzricje and Dusa.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: These were two villages just to the southwest of Gornji Vakuf. For the assault on the actual town of Gornji Vakuf itself, we believed that Colonel Siljeg had his forward headquarters, his tactical headquarters, situated in or near to a town -- a small village called Pidris, which was not far from both of those two towns. We believed that in order to have or to maintain the local security of his headquarters, that the Muslim population from those two villages was forcibly removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we did this morning, I'm going to show you a milinfosum report, 124, of the 3rd of March, 1993, the number being 520. Will you please examine the first page of that document, paragraph 1, relating to Gornji Vakuf, and could you confirm that the two villages we have mentioned are those appearing in this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, do you recall an artillery unit that called themselves Crnice Thunder in the Bugojno region? The Thunder of Crnice?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They were situated on a hill overlooking the town of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember something in particular regarding the way in which the guns of that unit were turned towards Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's common amongst mortar lines and artillery lines that when they are not actively engaging targets, they lay the guns on to what they consider to be their priority target or final protective fire. The guns of Crnice Thunder were laid on to the Muslim sector of Bugojno, so it would be fair to assume that they regarded that as their prime or final protective fire target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This manner of pointing guns towards a village is quite unusual; it is not part of military practice, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ordinarily, like I said, the guns were not in action. It's customary amongst all armies, when guns are not in action, they are laid on to your final protective fire. In a defensive position, the final protective fire would be just in front of your own soldiers' forward positions, so that if you were assaulted, you would be able to bring the fire down straightaway. The guns would already be laid on. It is unusual to have your final protective fire target as a civilian-occupied area of a town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you talk to us now about your mission of assistance and relief to a group of villagers in the villages of Bolkovac and Voljevac?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was tasked, as the patrol commander, to go and supervise the handover of a large group of civilians at a checkpoint just outside Gornji Vakuf. These civilians came from the two villages you just mentioned: Voljevac, Bolkovac. There were a mixture of children, old people, and women. Also, at the same checkpoint, at the same time, was a truck containing approximately a dozen dead Muslim militia, and one severely wounded Muslim militiaman stacked on top of the dead bodies. The women and children and old men had all obviously been mistreated. They were visibly distressed, they had no belongings, and they obviously did not wish to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember asking the commander of the HVO unit, who was present, why the wounded man, the Muslim person, had not been treated?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He said, "He's going to die anyway." He said he -- he said he hadn't been treated because he was going to die anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, able to give some treatment to this wounded person?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a heated exchange between me and the commander of the HVO unit at the checkpoint, and after about an hour, he finally agreed to allow me to remove the body -- or to remove the wounded man from the dead bodies, and I started to treat him at the side of the road and then summoned for proper army medical assistance, and we had him removed and taken to the Muslim first-aid post. He had severe shrapnel wounds in both legs, one of which was very, very infected. He was dehydrated, in shock, in a great deal of pain. I splinted one of his legs for him and injected him with my morphine syrette that every soldier carries around his neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the attitude taken by one of the HVO soldiers in relation to this wounded Muslim man?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: While I was treating him at the side of the road, one of the HVO soldiers prodded him with a bayonet and kept going, "Muslimski, Muslimski."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning, you mentioned the names of the various units fighting in the area for the HVO, and you mentioned the name of Nick Glasnovic as being the commander of the Tomislav Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That's correct. He's Canadian, a former -- he claimed to have also served in the French Foreign Legion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the citizenship of the second in command of that brigade? His name was Mr. Schmidt.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Schmidt was on formal secondment from the Croatian army. He was killed during fighting or the cleansing of -- one of the cleansing raids on Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke this morning of two units, the Bruno Busic Brigade and Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Bruno Busic unit had a special patch. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The detachment that was stationed in Gornji Vakuf was called the Alfa Forse, and their patch consisted -- one part of that patch consisted of an eagle with the words "Bruno Busic Alfa Forse".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony in May 1995, you provided a drawing of that patch. I'm going to show you the document issued at the time so that you can confirm whether that is the document. It is Z276.3, which I have already referred to this morning, but this time we are looking at page 1, 276.3, page 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the drawing that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You met the commander of that unit, Alfa Forse, that was stationed in Gornji Vakuf. Do you remember the kind of accessories he had to decorate the walls of his office with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He had a large World War II Nazi-style flag hanging behind his desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him why he had this flag in his office, and what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He said it was to annoy the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to talk now about the second brigade, the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade. Do you remember the insignia worn by that unit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a maple leaf or a leaf similar to a maple leaf and a sword or dagger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, you were able to note that within those units, Pavlovic and Bruno Busic, there were mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those units, were they equipped with the best military material at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They were better equipped and seemed better organised than the normal HVO brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your mission, you had opportunity to meet one of those mercenaries who came from Wales originally and belonged to the Bruno Busic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that mercenary?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: His real name was Llewellyn Thomas and his nom de guerre was Chris.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a former soldier of the British army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this mercenary told you that he was paid by the Croatian government in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he originally came to the Balkans and fought with the Croatian army, and as the war in Croatia wound down, the Croatian army sent him to the HVO. He was still paid by the Croatian government, his money was in the bank in Zagreb, and he had both a Croatian army and an HVO ID card.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another milinfo report, the 14th of March, 1993, document Z543.1. On page 2 of that report, which I should like you to look at, paragraph 5, "Gornji Vakuf," that a British mercenary was interviewed and provided certain information. Is this the mercenary you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Attached to this milinfosum, there is a report concerning the structure and the mission of the Bruno Busic Brigade. This is page 3 of that document. So could you look through it, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the information that was conveyed to you at the time by this mercenary?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That is the information that was published in the milinfosum. He also provided more information which was handed over separately, because the milinfosum was an open source of material, and some of the information that he provided us with was too sensitive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You dealt directly with this mercenary, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not the only mercenary that you met at the time. You spoke to us also about another mercenary called Carl or Charles Rutter. Do you remember that name?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Carl or Charles Rutter was a former soldier from my regiment and served in the same platoon as me in the early 1980s when we were based near London. On leave from the army, he became a professional mercenary, and he actually served in Bosnia twice with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, this mercenary, Carl or Charles Rutter, was he stationed in another part of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He fought near Gornji Vakuf, and he also fought in the big eruption of fighting that happened in Mostar the following year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of the information that you were able to obtain from these mercenaries and the commander of the Alfa Forse unit in Gornji Vakuf, were you able to conclude that these two units, Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic, were elite troops used by the HVO or shock troops?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The way it was explained to us was that the HVO consisted of locally raised brigades under the command of the various op zones and that there were two special brigades, the Bruno Busic Brigade and the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, which were brought in as reinforcements or to bolster things up and that they were a better type of soldier than the normal HVO soldier and that they were better motivated, better led, and they were used as sort of, yes, shock troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a new document, Mr. Williams. It is milinfosum number 163 of the 11th of April, 1993, referenced Z641.1. Could you please look at page 3 of that document, though it's numbered 2, it is actually page 3, and paragraph 6 relating to Gornji Vakuf, the last paragraph on this page, page number 3 really?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of this Alfa Forse unit, this gentleman, Ivica Budimir, is he mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the person who told you that these two units were used as some sort of strategic reserve?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He was the person who told us that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that those units represented the basis, the nucleus, of the future army of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. It was also what the mercenary, Llewellyn Thomas, said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself and your colleagues from the Cheshire Regiment were able to obtain information to show that these two units, Ludvig Pavlovic and Bruno Busic, were engaged in Vitez and in Novi Travnik; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your service follow the movement of these two units as they moved around the territory of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We used to monitor those two units in particular. They were what we called combat indicators. If they suddenly started appearing somewhere, then we knew that trouble would start very, very soon after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The French translation just said that you knew that things would happen very soon when they appeared somewhere. What things are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Usually a rapid rise in ethnic tensions and an outbreak of fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you four documents, four milinfosums, covering the period from the 9th of January, the 10th of January, and the 11th of January, 1993, and an milinfosum of the 23rd of April, 1993. These documents are D41/1 which is a document that the Defence has already tendered. The second is -- so D41/1, Z355.1. This is a document which was just produced this morning, Z355.1. I believe that the usher has it in his hands already. (In English) I think the usher has got this document in his hands. So Z355.1, Z355.2, and Z795.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Translation) As for the Document D45/1, page 4, Mr. Williams, could you please confirm to us if it deals with the movement of one of those units.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a movement of troops that we would have been monitoring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now will you look at 355.1, Z355.1. 355.1, page 3 and 4. Under 5, Novi Travnik, could you please tell us if this is indeed the same troop movement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the next page, page 4, that it is again those same units moving to Novi Travnik? It is the end of page 4.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next document, Z355.2, page 1, segment 3, about Vitez. Could you confirm to us that a soldier with this oak leaf or maple leaf on their patch are the ones addressed in this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on page 4, the last page of this document, could you confirm the information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That, again, that's referring, actually, to the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now will you look at document Z795, page 2, paragraph 4, relative to Gornji Vakuf. Did you write the last two sentences of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, to your knowledge, were these two units placed at the disposal of local HVO commanders?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The interpretation that we got was that they were a strategic reserve that was controlled from Mostar and would be brought into areas for specific operations. When not in use for those specific operations, they would slide -- for instance, the Alpha Forse that were in Gornji Vakuf would, on their normal day-to-day-type business, come under some form of operational command of the local brigade; but once they were tasked to do more important things, they would then be controlled directly from Mostar. For want of a better word, a sort of rapid reaction force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like you to look at another document, Z370. This document is an order signed by Colonel Blaskic, the commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia, of the 16th of January, 1993. You can see that among various things in this order, there are formations which are sort of addressed. There are two units specified, and these are Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic Brigades.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, how would you comment on this document? That is, the issue of such an order confirms the fact that these units could be placed at the disposal of local commanders; how would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It would appear on this particular document that the Ludvig Pavlovic and the Bruno Busic units that were subjected to this order had been seconded to the Op Zone Central Bosnia for a specific operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's one I'm looking at now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, we see that Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade is stationed in Vitez and Bruno Busic in Novi Travnik. Does this corroborate the information that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, we shall now move on to another subject. Do you remember Colonel Siljeg's reaction, and you spoke about him this morning, when, at a meeting with ECMM representatives, he asked me (sic) why were the soldiers of the 4th Split Brigade of the Croatian army fighting in the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: When Ambassador Bousseau asked Colonel Siljeg that, Colonel Siljeg just smiled and looked out of the window. He didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, he simply did not answer this question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He gave no answer at all. He didn't even shake or nod his head. He just smiled and then looked out of the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not deny it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He gave neither a denial nor a confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, in March 1993, did you, yourself, meet those soldiers from the 4th HVO Brigade, Split Brigade? Did you come across them in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I met a group of Croatian soldiers in Prozor, in the town centre. They were from the Croatian army and were wearing Croatian army insignia, a Tigers head badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were in uniforms, relevant uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed and in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you asked them why they were in Prozor, what did those soldiers tell you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They laughed and said they were there for a wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you accept this explanation as a serious explanation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We believed that it was a joke, and that the wedding was actually something to do with Herceg-Bosna and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will show you a report of the 20th of March, 1993, and it is the document Z557.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, there's a limit to the amount of paper that we can take in. Now, is there very much more coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is the last new document which I intended to produce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to look at page 3 of the report, paragraph 5, relating to the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. The third part of this paragraph concerns this meeting that you just mentioned, the soldiers of the 4th HV Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the same page, it seems that another unit from Croatia had been spotted in the region, the 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army. Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As I recall, they were -- it was actually me -- if it is the unit I think -- I recall it as being, it is a detachment of air defence soldiers that I met just outside of Bugojno town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Usher, you can take your seat again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your mission, Mr. Williams, you could see that the Croatian army had set up a military hospital in the village of Rumboci?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a military field hospital just on the edge of the village of Rumboci. I visited it on one occasion -- well, I visited it on more than one occasion, but on one occasion I actually spoke to the doctor, the surgeon that was there. He was in uniform. He identified himself to me as being from the Croatian army. When I asked him why he was in Rumboci if he was from the Croatian army, he told me that they regarded that part of Bosnia as being part of the Split military region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this hospital also equipped with a helicopter landing pad?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital was on the side of a sharp incline, and down on the field below it, they had a fully marked-out helicopter landing site. Casualties were flown from there -- they were patched up, the seriously injured ones were patched up and stabilised and then flown to Split for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also see what was the quality of the medical supplies used by the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was all very good condition, nearly all brand-new. Most of the drugs and medical-type supplies originated from Switzerland. Most of the equipment had originated from Austria and Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg asked you on one occasion if he could use the UNPROFOR landing site to transport his wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. He asked, during one of the conferences, he had some severely wounded soldiers. He needed to get them out of the area as fast as he could, and he wanted permission to use the HLS, helicopter landing site, that we had inside our base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those soldiers were then sent on to Split?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If we would have allowed it, presumably, yes, but we didn't allow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of your patrols met, in the beginning of 1993, a convoy of some three or four vehicles in the area, and one of them was particularly conspicuous because of a large antenna. Do you remember that encounter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Officially, we were not supposed to stop vehicles, but the patrol commander, his curiosity was aroused because of the number of antennas that particular vehicle had, and so we stopped it. There were a group of officers, military officers, in the vehicles, one of whom identified himself, or through one of his officers who could speak English identified himself, as being the commander of the Croatian military, which we took to mean that he was, in fact, General Bobetko, although he never said that he was General Bobetko. He just identified himself as the commander of the Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what this high officer looked like?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He's described as short, stocky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believed that those vehicles belonged to the Croatian army rather than the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There was a report in one of the big papers a couple of days later, because we used to get all the newspapers sent out from England, and it was either The Telegraph or The Times, but on that particular day, General Bobetko had been involved in a conference in Knin or with the autonomous Republic of Serbian Krajina. We believed at the time it was possible, because of the way the front line zigzagged over the routes and the accessibilities, et cetera, et cetera, that it may well have been General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This convoy was then blocked by your patrol. Whoever was responsible for this convoy, did he then contact your headquarters in Vitez in order to obtain authorisation to go on?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What happened was they used their own satellite phone to phone Vitez and ask Vitez -- or phone the HVO in Vitez to ask the HVO in Vitez to ask our headquarters in Vitez to ask our patrol to get out of the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the Bosnian Muslim forces in the area of Gornji Vakuf, during your mission there, you noted that there was a local brigade, which was the 308th Brigade, and also some soldiers who formally belonged to the Jajce Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also note the presence of other units or brigades of the BH army in that particular area in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall now ask you to read a document which was already produced before this Tribunal. It is the record of a press conference of January 1993, and it is Z382, and it was of January. Z382 and Z593. Will you please look at this document, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write here that on the day preceding the attack, the HVO attack on Gornji Vakuf, that the Muslim forces were concentrated in a particular sector. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. The only soldiers that were in Gornji Vakuf were the soldiers from Gornji Vakuf and the remnants of the Jajce Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many were there, the soldiers of the former Jajce Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Approximately 50 of them, and they lived in the villages of Bolkovac and Voljevac. There were probably more scattered about in places as far away as Zenica and things like that, but in the Gornji Vakuf area, there were just the 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher, you may go back to your seat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, during your mission there, did you receive any information that would be indicating that Dario Kordic played or did not play a role in these conflicts which took place in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, he had no direct influence in what was happening around Gornji Vakuf at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the accused, Dario Kordic, mentioned during the months of your tour there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anybody refer to the accused, Dario Kordic, during the months that you stayed there in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was a known personality, but he was not, to my knowledge, active in my area. His activities were more along Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it that you learned about him? What kind of information reached you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was a very, very influential figure within the HDZ in Central Bosnia, part of the actual HDZ hierarchy for the whole of the Croatian area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "HDZ," do you mean the Croat party?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Croat party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know if he had a particular duty, if he played a particular role in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, he was either the political leader or very nearly the political leader of the Central Bosnian region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you know what kind of relationship existed between Dario Kordic and Mate Boban, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He was referred to as Mate Boban's right-hand man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the second accused, Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have never heard of --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard the name. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What information did you get about him when you heard him referred to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Again, he was an influential figure in the HDZ setup. He was more in Central Bosnia and not my area. My area was Gornji Vakuf, which was more Herzegovina than Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, my name is Steve Sayers. I represent Dario Kordic. You have been a most accommodating witness, so we will try to get you out of here at the end of the day, if possible. Let me explain to you one endemic problem that we have here. We both speak the same language, so it's very important to make sure that there's a pause between the question and the answer, and it's important for me to ensure that there's a pause between the answer and the next question; otherwise the translators get behind and it's not really fair to them. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Williams, you were the Colour Sergeant in the 1st Cheshire Regiment stationed with Bravo Company in the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were responsible for the milinfocell that was operated by the Bravo Company in your immediate area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that Sergeant Connelly, back at brigade headquarters in Vitez, was essentially in charge of the information gathering activities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, because he was actually from the intelligence corps. It was the battle group headquarters. The brigade headquarters was in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The person that was responsible for reviewing and authorising the final version, if you like, of the milinfosums, for example, would be Captain Chris Leyshon, I understand?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The battle headquarters of your regiment was actually located in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that there was another detachment of soldiers with the Dutch Battalion actually stationed in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, I would like to say that you have a spectacular recall of names and troop dispositions, it's very impressive, but do you speak Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I do not speak Croatian, no. I only have firsthand knowledge of what I was talking about of what happened in Gornji Vakuf, and because I was there and I wrote it and I wrote it down at the time, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Did you use translators at all in your dealings with both Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. We had two interpreters from the civil population, and we also had an officer who spoke Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Captain Nick Short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Williams, you arrived in Central Bosnia in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left with your regiment on May the 10th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I left slightly before that. I left about May the 4th or 5th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would it be fair to say that during the course of your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, sir, that the whole reason for UNPROFOR and BritBat being in the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1994 was because there was a terrible and bloody civil war raging in the country between three ethnic factions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That was the reason why UNPROFOR was there, but UNPROFOR's actual role was to escort humanitarian relief to where it was needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was your initial mission statement --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The war had nothing to do with us or we were not to get directly involved in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already spoken about the strategic significance of the main supply route that ran, I think you said, from Prozor up through Gornji Vakuf to Bugojno and points north?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf sat astride the route that went up through to Bugojno, but it also sat astride the route that went up through to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Gornji Vakuf essentially controlled two important strategic routes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's no question of the military significance, the importance of Gornji Vakuf as a choke point, to use a phrase?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, from a military perspective, at least, that if someone controlled this town, they also controlled the roads?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, they would control the access to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions generally about the intelligence gathering process. We've already heard from your commanding officer up until January of 1993, Major Rule, and he informed us that you had great experience in the intelligence gathering process. Would you say that's a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Information gathering and processing. Intelligence is the finished product at the other end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were told, I believe, to gather as much information as possible and then to collate it, analyse it, and report it in what would ultimately become milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the purpose of these milinfosums was to pass on all valuable and important military information up to the battle group headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically, you presided over that task in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these milinfosums are regularly consulted by your colleagues and by officers to inform themselves about what is going on in various areas?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's used as one of -- it was used as one of several sources of information of what was going on in various areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have a few questions more on this subject. You mentioned that milinfosums are one of several sources. Would you also agree that daily situation reports would be another one of those sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, along with the UNHCR representatives who drove around the country, and other agencies like that. We would use everything that we could, and cross-reference it and compare it and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually receive from the UNHCR and other organisations that you've referred to --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were other reports that came from other organisations, but I cannot remember which ones actually produced paper ones and which ones it was just verbal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a regular practice to draft documents known as orbats, or orders of battle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe that those provide a sort of a structured graphic detail relating to the subordination of units and also to personalities of the various warring factions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and it would then be used -- the orbats would be used by various other agencies so that they knew who to ask for when they were in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These orbats would be distributed to organisations that would have an interest in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, organisations such as the ECMM, European Community Military Monitors, and people like that. Likewise, they used to supply us with bits and pieces of the orbat, and together we would just cobble it all together and make a proper one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were updated on a relatively regular basis, every month or so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The -- we also had a team of liaison officers who would visit brigade commanders and other personalities. As personalities were promoted or moved to different jobs or whatever, they would update that. And in fact, if you read through all the milinfosums, you will see that it will say sometimes, the new commander of is, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever, yourself, obtain any information about the disposition of HVO forces in the town of Busovaca, for example?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. Busovaca was Central Bosnia; it was not my area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a completely different Operative Zone, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO troops in your Operative Zone were included in the command of the Northwest Herzegovina Operative Zone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Or so we believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did you also -- or did BritBat prepare, on a fairly regular basis, maps called disposition of warring factions maps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, with the front line, recent incidents that had happened. They were basically a visual briefing aid for the soldiers, something that they could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these would actually be given to the soldiers in order to facilitate an understanding of significant events or the disposition of the actual competent factions in their area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah. They were pinned up on the wall for the soldiers to look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those maps are different, I take it, from the current situation maps which were produced weekly by the battle group headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was -- you obviously know the map itself, but there were several different variants of it. The base map was the same, but you could get different types. Some would show ethnic breakdowns, some would show the routes, some would show the front lines, some would show recent incidents, and things like that. There were different variants of the same map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two final questions with respect to the milinfosums. Anything which could be described as affecting the provision of humanitarian aid, which was your primary mission, would be something that would be considered sufficiently important to put into a milinfosum; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah. Blockages of the route, shelling of the route, or mining of it; whatever. Things like that, where the routes were closed down, either permanently or temporarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the sorts of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the kinds of information that would routinely be included in milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. The location of checkpoints, we monitor the checkpoints, because sometimes the checkpoints would not allow vehicles to move through, and things like that. So we used to monitor the locations of checkpoints, how many soldiers were on them, what sort of weaponry they had. A sudden increase in the number of soldiers on a checkpoint would indicate that they were going to clamp down in some way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, when you were a sergeant in the British army in Central Bosnia, sir, that you found yourself confronted with a confusing and complex situation, militarily and ethnically and politically?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. At the very start, we were blind. We were the first unit to go. Nobody had been before. We were the first British unit to go, and so we had to build everything from scratch, basically, and so at the very beginning, an awful lot of information gathering was targeted at trying to find out who the local commanders were, where the troops were, even where the front line was, because we weren't too sure where the front line was at the start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately prior to your arrival in Gornji Vakuf, did you understand that the town of Jajce had been captured as a result of a Serb offensive?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That resulted in a huge efflux of refugees from the Jajce area into Central Bosnia and down into your area, in Gornji Vakuf, as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Serb offensive resulted in very heavy shelling of the city of Jajce; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It happened just before we deployed, and so I don't really -- other than watching it on television in Germany just before we went, and the commanding officer having to rethink his plans, because he hadn't planned -- as he had worked his deployment plan out to deploy the battalion, he had worked on the front line as it was then, and now the front line had moved quite significantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the local population had swelled to as of, say, March the 29th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The local population of where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Gornji Vakuf area, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I would assume it would be -- for the whole opstina, do you mean, or just the town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one at a time. We have previously stipulated in this case that before the civil war broke out, the opstina population was 25.131. And "opstina" refers to the --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
