utterances.text: -- municipality around the sort of county seat, if you like, Gornji Vakuf. And the town population, at least according to the 1991 census, was 5.344. I don't know that we need to burden the Trial Chamber with too much more paper, but let me just read you from milinfosum 150 on the 29th of March, 1993. It says, "B Company" -- this is on page 1 -- "reported that the population was now approximately 60.000" --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That would be for the whole opstina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- right -- "of whom one-third were refugees." So about 20.000 refugees. Is that pretty much consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: There were a lot of refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Turning to a different subject, sir, the chain of command that you've given some testimony about, was it your understanding that the central headquarters of the HVO military forces was in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commander in chief of the Bosnian Croat armed forces was, I think you've previously stated, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. He was either the commander in chief or the chief of staff, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that the commander of the Northwest Herzegovina Operative Zone and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone both reported directly to Brigadier Petkovic in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commanding officer of the Northwest Herzegovina Operative Zone, I think you've previously testified, was Colonel Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Colonel Siljeg, the gentleman with the eyebrows, actually did get married in March of 1993 in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not know that. I know he had a girlfriend, because he used to bring his girlfriend to the peace talks, and she wore a uniform. But I did not know he got married in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have stated that the name of the brigade stationed in Gornji Vakuf was the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the CO of the brigade, I believe, was Zrinko Tokic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he be the person that you would normally go to or that your commanding officer --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The actual person who, on the day-to-day business, where the OC wanted to speak or the liaison officer wanted to speak, they normally spoke to the 2IC, Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luka Sekerija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the commanding officer of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Colonel Tihomir Blaskic was the person that we had down on the orbat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have seen him once. I had him pointed out to me, and I have also seen a photograph of him in Colonel Stewart's book. I didn't go to Vitez that often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It was a one-hour drive, and it was -- too many hierarchy around there. We tried to stay out of the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as being rather dangerous. Did you ever meet Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic personally?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have seen him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony about various people faxing materials to locations that had a Split prefix?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, a Split area code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same thing with respect to INMARSAT telephone calls, I believe?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to whom those items were faxed or the persons to whom the telephone calls were made?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a foreign press bureau located in Split?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I did not know. Split was our brigade headquarters. That was two levels above me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conclusion, in the statement that you gave a few years ago, Mr. Williams, was that Brigadier General Petkovic was intimately and personally involved in making military decisions in the Gornji Vakuf area throughout your tour. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: He would -- as overall commander, he would be responsible for making decisions regarding HVO military activity throughout the whole of Bosnia. However, when the fighting was at its peak in Gornji Vakuf, he was involved directly then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The intelligence and information sources available to you gave you no assistance in determining to whom these faxes were sent and the telephone calls were made, I take it; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yeah. All I did was print -- got the machine to print the numbers out and sent the numbers further up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that throughout your time in Central Bosnia, sir, that Split was actually a central logistics centre and base for supplies into Central Bosnia and into your area as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have to be, because of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And it would be fair to say, as well, I think, that it would have been used as such by not only the Bosnian Croats, but also the Bosnian Muslims too?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. It would be fair to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by UNPROFOR as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very busy road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had spoken about two incidents that, in your view, sparked or provided the immediate spark to the fighting that broke out in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993, and one of them was an incident in which a person was beheaded by a sheet of glass, I believe. Do you know whether that was a handicapped person or a mentally retarded child?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The victim had a disability of some sort, be it either he was a paraplegic or mentally retarded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say that that is simply what was related to you? In other words -- let me see if I can rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What was told to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Our OC at the time, Major Rule, was actively involved in trying to defuse -- they very nearly went to war over that. Both sides got the weapons out, and they were tooling up, ready to go, and our OC got both commanders in and managed to defuse the situation, but there was an awful lot of antagonism over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not actually see the incident yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or its aftermath, other than the negotiations aftermath?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. There was no denial that it happened, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it also be fair to say that once the fighting actually did break out in January of 1993, that the local population from both sides, Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim, went to arms?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was -- the initial fighting was the local -- the locals from both sides. Both commanders, the Muslim commander and the HVO commander, knew each other and were both very distressed by what was going on, and did try their hardest to stop it at the start, but then externals got involved, and it just snowballed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also provided some testimony about the arrest of the culprit in this incident and his supposed sighting in combat on the front lines at some point later. Did you, yourself, see this gentleman back on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I didn't, but the Muslims repeatedly brought it up during the ceasefire negotiations, and the Bosnian Croats did not deny it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave some testimony about military police operations conducted in the village of -- forgive my pronunciation -- Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's probably better pronounced than I pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these units yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We saw the units moving around. I did not actually see those units do that particular thing, but those units were there. We saw them at the side of the road before it and after it, and we saw them moving around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And basically you put in the milinfosums what had been reported to you by Muslim sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Muslim sources, patrols, what I'd seen, what the liaison officers had seen, and in fact also from Croatian sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the testimony that you gave regarding the 4th Brigade of the Croatian army, or the 20 or so people that you saw from that brigade, are you sure that it was the 4th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The insignia that they wore gave the impression that it was -- that the number was 4 Brigade. It was a tiger's head, which I believe actually is linked to the 1st Brigade as opposed to the 4th Brigade, but the insignia they wore was 4 Brigade. They said they were Croatian soldiers from the Croatian army. They had "HV" as opposed to "HVO" insignia, and the difference between them and HVO was marked, very noticeable. They were proper soldiers and not what we used to call -- well, without being derogatory, we used to refer to the HVO as Mickey Mouse soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be fair to say -- and there's been testimony on this; I don't think there is any disagreement that the HVO military units and the BiH military units could be seen in a wide variety of --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- attire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A wide variety of weapons, a wide variety of wearing their equipment. No set pattern of uniformity. The HVO were probably more -- were less tatty than the Muslim soldiers, but they were tatty nonetheless. But these were different; the difference in these was marked. They were proper soldiers, from a proper army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these soldiers told you, in a jovial manner, that they were in town for a marriage?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: A wedding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A wedding; I'm sorry. Did you ever see these soldiers engaged in combat activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, but they were armed to the teeth. It's slightly strange attire to wear for a wedding: full uniform, 5,56 millimetre Austrian Sig rifles, all the gear, backpacks, sleeping bags. Some wedding, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But pretty sensible gear to wear if you're in the middle of a civil war; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Prozor was a fairly peaceful town. It occasionally got shelled, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave some testimony about a Croatian hospital in Rumboci?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any Muslim wounded were treated at that hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have no idea. I didn't ask who he treated at all. I just asked where he was from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that during the fighting in Gornji Vakuf in January, I believe it erupted on the 14th or 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: It's hard to put an exact time and date that it started because it was sporadically ongoing at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Muslim forces in that town gave a pretty good account of themselves?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: They gave a very good account of themselves. There again, they were surrounded. They weren't going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have previously given some testimony about the numerous ceasefire negotiations and agreements, or lack of agreements. Did you ever see a general ceasefire agreement that was issued on January the 20th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I am aware of its existence, but at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you need to see it, we'll be happy to show it to you, but would it be fair to say that that was an agreement signed on behalf of the Bosnian Croat military by Brigadier Petkovic and by the Muslim forces, the 4th Corps, under the signature of Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I know the document that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, the order actually states that the senseless conflict in the Gornji Vakuf area has got to come to an immediate stop; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that with the exception of sporadic gunfire, the general violence, the general open warfare, if you like, in Gornji Vakuf in January of 1993 gradually petered out in February, March, and April?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, it became calmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, the fighting that erupted in the Lasva Valley in the middle of April 1993 did not actually spread over into your area of responsibility. Your area of responsibility remained relatively peaceful and calm during that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At that particular time, we had undertaken the role of police in Gornji Vakuf, and so our presence was on the ground all the time. We had checkpoints out in the town, foot patrols, all this sort of stuff, to underpin the ceasefire agreement in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question in connection with the ceasefire agreement that we've just been talking about: One of the arrangements that was reached between the formally competent forces, the Croats and the Muslims, was for the dismantling of all fortifications in the town and for the filling in of defensive positions, such as trenches; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, UNPROFOR, specifically the forces in your detachment, Bravo Company, oversaw the implementation of those arrangements, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were pretty successfully concluded, I think you would agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to my final series of questions: Since I represent Mr. Kordic, I think you will anticipate that I would ask some questions about him. I don't believe you've met him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I've seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've never met him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Not formally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In the Gornji Vakuf area, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on the television or hear him on the radio?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I've seen him in newspapers, I've seen photographs of him, I've seen one brief clip of him on television, and I saw him once in reality, just somebody pointed him out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've agreed that, as far as you could determine with all the means of information and intelligence available to you, he had absolutely no involvement in local decisions, local military decisions, as far as you were concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: For my area, as far as I'm aware, he had no major decisions -- he had no major role to play. That's as far as I'm aware. It was more of a Central Bosnia sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, as my final question, that you really don't know anything specific about Mr. Kordic at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Other than he was a very, very high ranking person in the HDZ and was referred to as Mate Boban's right-hand man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referred to by whom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The milinfosums and the verbal briefings that we used to go to. Once a week, I had to go to Vitez for a verbal briefing, and they would talk about -- we would talk through things with various other people. In fact, in Mr. Kordic's case, he did not come to my attention, because he was not from my area, until probably -- as I started to pay more and more attention to what was starting to happen up in Central Bosnia, which would probably be late January onwards, is when I started to notice his name more and more often, because other than that, what happened up in Central Bosnia was really not my area, and so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say then that the information that you received that he was, to use your phrase, "Mate Boban's right-hand man," was information that you received from your colleagues rather than from Bosnian Croats or from local people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The actual expression "Mate Boban's right-hand man," as I recall, came from an ECMM monitor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- who worked out of Grude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's basically all that you've told the Trial Chamber that you know about Mr. Kordic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that he was pointed out to you. In what circumstances was he pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If you were up in Vitez, if people were knocking about, we used to go for drive-arounds and things like that, and you might see the local brigade commander somewhere, and I might have, say, somebody from Vitez with me, and I would say, "That's Zrinko Tokic," sort of thing. It was just a personality. He was just pointed out to me as Dario Kordic. It was not, "That's Dario Kordic, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah," just "That's Dario Kordic." It would be the equivalent of, say, if you were out shopping and you saw a film star and somebody said, "Oh, that's so and so."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you any questions? Mr. Mikulicic, we are running fairly late, and we must adjourn at twenty past. Can you finish by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I'm aware of the shortness of time, but I will need even less time than you envisage, I assure you. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Williams. I am Mikulicic, attorney from Zagreb, and in this case, I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. I have a few questions for you and will be done very soon. You have already told us unequivocally, during your testimony today, that the area of Vitez and Busovaca was the area of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and that this Operative Zone was not your area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, from this area of Central Bosnia, did any people come to negotiate a ceasefire in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Mr. Williams, what is the distance in kilometres between Gornji Vakuf and Vitez, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The actual road distance, I couldn't tell you, but it used to take an hour in an armoured vehicle to drive, which is why nobody used to like going there. So I would have to say that it is probably in the region of 30 kilometres, maybe slightly more, maybe slightly less, but it took an hour in an armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though I realise that the area of Vitez did not belong to your field of interest, I shall ask you whether you know some people from Vitez. Do you know somebody called Ivica Santic or have you heard anything about him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Is it, what, Santic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Santic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marijan or Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No. I did not -- it was not my area, so you could probably get somebody from Vitez and ask them about people in Gornji Vakuf and they wouldn't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now ask you the same question that my colleague, Mr. Sayers, put to you, as I represent Mr. Cerkez. Answering his question, you said that you knew, and I will quote, "an influential person in the HDZ." Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Can you say that again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When answering a question put to you by the Prosecutor and when the Prosecutor asked you whether you had heard of a man called Mario Cerkez, you said that you didn't know him but that you had heard that he was an influential person in the HDZ. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I have seen his name on paper, and as I recall, it was linked to him being an influential person within the Bosnian Croat community, the HDZ. Other than that, that is only as I recall. He's not somebody that springs to mind for me. For instance, I know Colonel Blaskic by name. I've seen him once. I've seen pictures of him. But Colonel Siljeg, I actually know like this, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Williams, for you: Could you please tell me what the term "HDZ" means to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: "HDZ" is a political party, Bosnian Croat political party, very closely linked to the HVO, which is the Bosnian Croat defence force. There is a lot of overlap between the two or we believed at the time that there was a lot of overlap between the two. You could say that the HDZ is the political wing of the HVO or you could say that the HVO is the military wing of the HDZ, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So the most important thing is that when you say "HDZ," you mean a political party of the Bosnian Croats; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, but they are side-by-side organisations that overlap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A single question, Mr. President, one only. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, in connection with those telephone calls -- there seems to be a translation problem?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: No, it's coming through fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with those telephone calls made by General Petkovic and the use of the telecopying machine by Colonel Siljeg, you confirm that your telephone and your telecopier were being used in the middle of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your understanding at the time was that those messages were being sent to solicit possible instructions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. There seemed to be no decisions made until after a phone call. They talked, a phone call, then a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your interpretation is quite that it wasn't a question of calling Mrs. Petkovic or Mrs. Siljeg, but rather calling the offices in Split?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Well, calling somewhere with a Split area code for instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At 9.00 tomorrow. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
